description: Team Argo is building a lunar landing site planner for the Moon's south pole: a web app that lets mission planners compare sites and dates at a glance, with Sun and Earth positions against the real terrain horizon, power and comms windows on one timeline, and a 3D terrain view that shows why the numbers look the way they do.
summary:
Argo is a web app for choosing where and when to land on the Moon. Pick a site and a date, and it tells you whether a solar panel there gets sunlight and whether Earth is above the horizon for direct radio contact, both at any moment and over the first 30 days after touchdown.

Near the lunar south pole the Sun stays within a few degrees of the horizon, so a ridge a few kilometres away can decide whether a lander has power. Argo traces the real horizon around each site from LOLA elevation data and compares it with the Sun’s and Earth’s positions. We checked those positions against 110 NASA JPL Horizons cases, and the largest error is 0.0033°.

A sky chart shows when the terrain blocks the Sun or Earth. A 3D view rebuilds the terrain around the site and lights it from where the Sun really is, so the shadows fall where they would on that date. Compare puts up to three sites or dates side by side, and Nudge finds nearby spots or dates that add more hours of power and contact.

A lander that touches down in shadow, or out of contact with Earth, can lose its mission in hours. Argo lets a planner test candidate sites and dates for this before committing to one.
details:
What it does

Argo answers one question for a lunar landing: if we land here on this date, will the solar panel get sunlight, and will Earth be above the horizon for direct radio contact? It also says for how long.

You pick a place and a time. The place can be one of 20 sites (south pole candidates such as Shackleton rim, Connecting Ridge, de Gerlache rim and Malapert Massif, plus past landings from Apollo 11 to Chandrayaan-3, Chang’e, SLIM and Intuitive Machines), any latitude and longitude, or a pin dropped on the globe. Argo then shows:

  • At this moment: Sun and Earth elevation above the local horizon, panel power, whether the Earth link is up, and the time to the next sunset or Earthset.
  • Over the window: sunlit share, Earth-in-view share, power plus link share, and the longest dark spell, with a timeline you can scrub or play.
  • Sky chart: the Sun’s and Earth’s paths drawn over the site’s horizon silhouette, so you can see which ridge blocks them and when. A table view lists the exact angles.
  • 3D site: a 20 km square of terrain around the site, lit from the Sun’s true direction, with Earth placed where it really is in the sky.
  • Compare: up to three sites or landing dates scored over the first 30 days after touchdown: hours with power and contact, first unbroken window, time until the Sun is lost, and longest dark.
  • Nudge: tests 16 spots 1 to 2 km away and landing up to 3 days earlier or later, then lists the changes that add the most hours.

Every scenario is stored in the URL, so a result can be shared as a link.

How it works

Sun and Earth positions come from astronomy-engine, using the IAU rotation model for the Moon including libration. Positions are topocentric, so the observer’s height and parallax are included. Both bodies are treated as discs, not points (the Sun is about 0.27° across in radius terms, Earth about 1°). A panel’s power depends on how much of the Sun’s disc clears the horizon.

The horizon is computed for 720 directions, one every 0.5°. For each one, Argo marches outward to 200 km over LOLA elevation data (40 m grid near the site, 240 m further out) and keeps the highest angle, including the Moon’s curvature. Sites away from the pole use SLDEM2015 from LOLA and Kaguya. Custom points in the south polar region use the 240 m grid. Elsewhere they fall back to a smooth sphere, and the app says so.

We checked the engine against 110 NASA JPL Horizons cases (DE441) at 9 sites and 6 dates. The largest error is 0.0033°, against a Sun radius of about 0.27°. The Apollo 11 landing moment matches Horizons to 0.001°.

Tools

  • App: TypeScript, React, Vite
  • 3D: three.js with React Three Fiber
  • Animation and state: GSAP, Zustand
  • Astronomy: astronomy-engine for Sun, Earth and Moon positions
  • Data processing: Python with NumPy and Pillow, which bakes the terrain and horizons offline, so the browser loads small files and the core app needs no server
  • Testing: Vitest
  • Hosting: Cloudflare Pages

Benefits and impact

At the south pole the Sun never rises more than about 1.6° above a flat horizon, so a ridge a few kilometres away can decide whether a lander has power. Getting a site or date wrong can mean landing in shadow or out of contact. Argo lets mission planners, students and space agencies check candidate sites in seconds instead of running a custom analysis. The 30-day compare and Nudge views show what a small change in site or date is worth in hours.

What is new

The sky chart puts the real terrain silhouette behind the Sun and Earth tracks, so the reason for each sunset or loss of signal is visible. The 3D shadows and the numbers come from the same horizon, so they agree. Compare shows each figure on its own row and marks the best one. There is no blended score hiding the trade-offs.

What we considered

The Assumptions panel in the app lists the limits:

  • The ME frame used by LOLA and the IAU frame used by the engine differ by about 100 m on the surface. We measured the effect on angles and it stays within the 0.0033° above.
  • Terrain closer than 200 m is ignored, because the 40 m grid can’t resolve it.
  • Horizons are baked for a 2 m mast.
  • There is no refraction, because the Moon has no atmosphere.

The app works on phones, supports keyboard use, and opens with an optional tour for first-time users.
